catalog_quote: [Dettweiler 2015:34-35] C'Lela has two levels of lexical tone, namely high [H] and low [L]. This is illustrated in (223) for monosyllabic noun roots and in (224) for disyllabic noun roots. Note the minimal pairs in (223e & k) showing emic contrast between [gé] 'river' and [gè] 'species of tree', with H and L tone patterns respectively. ... Another feature of C'Lela is the occurrence, primarily in disyllabic noun roots, of a falling [HL] tone. The distribution of the HL tone appears to be restricted as follows: 1. It is almost always in a word-final CV syllable where the V is phonetically long (vowel length was confirmed with speech analyzer software). 2. The preceding (penultimate) syllable is always low tone. 3. The penultimate syllable is almost always either a CVC syllable, or a CV syllable with a long vowel in the nucleus ... new_statements.rule_in_words: All accessible first-hand descriptions analyse C'lela as a register-tone language (H, L, plus a restricted falling HL on long final syllables after a low penult; grammatical tone in verb inflection). None of them states where word stress falls or whether a word accent exists; the only use of the word 'stress' is Aliero's comparative remark that C'lela does not use (compound) stress to distinguish compounds from phrases. No positive or negative word-stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule given). Tone-related distributional facts only: falling HL almost always on a word-final CV syllable with phonetically long vowel, preceded by a low, usually heavy (CVC or CVV) penult (Dettweiler 2015:35-36); heavy syllable types concentrate in root-initial syllables (2015:18-19).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on noun/verb roots in citation form (Zuru dialect) and grammatical tone in verbal morphology; falling tone described as phrase-final in Dettweiler 2012 App. A.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Zuru dialect of C'lela (the reference dialect chosen for writing; Dettweiler 2000 fn., Dettweiler 2015 sec.1.3), i.e. the language-level languoid clel1238 [dri]; older literature calls it Dakarkari/Dakarci/Lela.

sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology (pp.13-41) covers phonemes, syllable/word patterns, vowel length, morphophonology, lexical tone (sec.2.8, p.34: two level tones H and L plus a restricted falling HL) and grammatical tone (sec.2.9). The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the book; no statement on word stress.

sources.note: Sec.1.4.2 phonology preliminaries; 1.4.2.6 'Tone' (p.19-20): 'C'lela, like many other African languages, is a tone language' with H, L and a falling tone, lexical and grammatical function. Only stress remark is comparative/negative (p.179): 'C'lela, unlike English, does not use stress in distinguishing a compound from a phrase'. No statement of where word stress falls or whether it exists; refers readers to Dettweiler 2001, 2012a for phonology.
